title: Justice Department Steps Up Cases Against Trump Foes Days Before Midterms
excerpt: A third prosecution of James Comey, a search of Rep. Ilhan Omar's home and charges against two former FBI officials have former prosecutors questioning a break with pre-election practice.
body:
• The Justice Department has opened or escalated cases against several Trump critics in the final weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, including a third prosecution of former FBI director James Comey.
  • Federal agents searched the Washington home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, and prosecutors charged two former FBI officials over testimony about investigations involving Hunter Biden.
  • Former prosecutors say the pace breaks with the department's long-standing practice of avoiding headline-making actions close to an election; the department says filing a criminal information is a recognized practice and declined further comment on the Comey case.
  • For US voters, including Indian-American voters, the cases land as control of Congress is decided on November 3 — and several of the legal fights will be resolved by judges, not voters.

The Justice Department has moved against a series of President Donald Trump's political opponents in the final stretch before next week's midterm elections, in what the Wall Street Journal described as a frenzy of legal maneuvers over the past two weeks. Federal authorities searched the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, a frequent Trump critic. Prosecutors initiated a third prosecution of former FBI director James Comey. FBI director Kash Patel announced charges against two former FBI intelligence officials, alleging they lied to Congress about their roles in investigations of Hunter Biden.

The department also tried and failed to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson over testimony she gave to Congress more than four years ago linking Trump to the January 6, 2021 violence at the US Capitol, the Journal reported. Former federal prosecutors and legal observers told the Journal the actions show signs of being rushed, with uncommon legal maneuvers and cases built on years-old claims. Two of the matters were charged without the involvement of grand juries.

The third case against Comey

The newest Comey case surfaced on Monday in unsealed court documents, the Associated Press reported. Prosecutors accuse Comey of a decade-old leak of classified information connected to an October 2016 New York Times story about a secret court order requiring Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization.

https://x.com/OwenGregorian/status/2115075125015953562

The department filed a criminal information — a charging document that does not require a grand jury vote — under seal on October 5. A department spokesperson said filing an information to extend, or toll, the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice approved by multiple appeals courts, and declined further comment because the investigation is ongoing.

Comey's lawyers argue the filing is invalid. They say the law requires an indictment voted by a grand jury within the 10-year statute of limitations, and that the same allegation was investigated twice before — by prosecutor John Durham, who recommended no charges in 2018, and by the US Attorney's office in Washington, which closed its inquiry in 2020 without charges.

"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice — one that we cannot become numb to. I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people."

— James Comey, former FBI director

This is the third criminal case against Comey since Trump returned to the White House. A Virginia case accusing him of lying to Congress in 2020 was dismissed after a judge found the prosecutor was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment accuses him of threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells arranged as "86 47." On Monday, a judge also ruled the department had illegally fired Comey's daughter Maurene, a New York prosecutor, last year.

A break with pre-election practice

The timing is the core of the dispute. The department has long observed an informal 60-to-90-day period of heightened caution before elections, avoiding public steps that could affect voting. The Associated Press reported that defense lawyers, Democrats and other critics say the October blitz is no coincidence, pointing to both timing and targets.

The department's position, as stated in the Comey matter, is procedural: the filing method is recognized, the investigation is ongoing, and it will not comment further. The case against the two former FBI officials is already being tested in court, the Journal reported.

What happens next

The immediate decisions sit with judges. Comey's lawyers have asked a judge to dismiss the new information, and that request is pending. The charges against the former FBI officials face continued hearings. The Omar search has not, in the reporting to date, produced a public charge.

Voters go to the polls on November 3 with control of Congress at stake. Whatever the courts decide will come after the election. The cases — and the argument over making them this close to one — are now part of the campaign's final week.
